Home News Arts and Culture Business Sports Opinion Research Live TV/Radio Media Elections Dark Mode Dark mode --> Bola Ray featured in GQ Poland, says Africa is not the next big thing, Africa is now 17 November 2026 2:53pm ▶ Listen to this article Audio By Carbonatix
Renowned media mogul and CEO of EIB Network, Nathan Kwabena Anokye Adisi, popularly known as Bola Ray, has been featured in the 2026 edition of GQ Poland's GQ Business magazine in a wide-ranging interview titled "Własnym głosem" ("In His Own Voice").
The multi-page feature, published in the magazine's Business World section, was conducted by Omenaa Mensah, founder of the Omenaa Art Foundation, Omenaa Foundation and TOP CHARITY, with photography by Jacek Poremba. It traces Bola Ray's journey from student radio DJ to head of one of Ghana's leading media groups.
He told the magazine that he began his career in the late 1990s as a volunteer at Radio Universe at the University of Ghana, where he studied management.
He explained that his stage name came about when he entered Accra Academy at age 11. "Bola" stands for "brilliant, outstanding, loving, ambitious," while "Ray" stands for "religious, ambitious, young."
He said he set out to become the biggest DJ in Ghana and the first with a degree, at a time when many believed the profession was for people without formal education.
On the continent's place in the world, Bola Ray said Africa is largely undiscovered and has many stories to tell, and he urged foreign media to give it far more attention.
He said the world hears too often about hunger, war, poverty and disease, when Africa is a jewel of enormous potential. He asked why stories of Afrobeats conquering the world, and of Africa's music and creative industries, are not told more often.
"There are reports saying Africa is 'the next big thing.' I disagree. Africa is now," he said.
He pointed to the continent's natural resources, including lithium, cocoa, gold and diamonds, and called on industrialists and entrepreneurs to build factories in Africa to add value locally.
Bola Ray said he would like to see genuine collaboration among African media houses in countries such as Nigeria, Ghana, South Africa and Kenya, working together each week to select the most important African story and share it with their audiences.
He noted that the media is no longer limited to traditional companies, as anyone with a phone can tell the story of their community, culture or place.
He also stressed the need to showcase success stories from Africa and the diaspora, which inspired him to create the television programme Revealed .
"We cannot talk endlessly about politics. We must tell positive stories as well," he said.
He observed that Africans have for years been taught not to talk too much about their achievements for fear of seeming arrogant, and said he wants experienced African entrepreneurs to share their stories with young people.
"It is good to appear in Western media, but it is equally important to tell these stories here," he said.
Bola Ray also spoke about the Omenaa Sport & Art Campus in Tema, which opened in October, and praised Omenaa Mensah for an initiative that supports young talent in Africa. He said he wants young people to meet artists, entrepreneurs and others who can become role models.
"It is not about boasting of success, but about showing them what is possible," he said.
